subject: Ch2: Lexical Analysis (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on tokens/lexemes/patterns, regular expressions and identities, finite automata, RE→NFA→DFA, subset construction, DFA minimization, longest-match/lookahead, and the limits of regular languages.

questions.text: Applying subset construction to an NFA with n states can, in the worst case, yield a DFA with:
options: At most n^2 states, because pairs of NFA states form the DFA states
Up to 2^n states
Exactly the same n states, since each NFA state maps to one DFA state
Always strictly fewer than n states once unreachable subsets are pruned
questions.shortExplanation: DFA states are subsets of NFA states → up to 2^n.
questions.explanation: Each DFA state corresponds to a set of NFA states, so the number of DFA states can be as large as the number of subsets, 2^n, in the worst case.

questions.text: The regular expression `(a|b)*abb` denotes the set of strings over {a,b} that:
options: End in abb
Have even length and an equal number of a's and b's
Contain exactly one occurrence of the letter b and any number of a's
Start with the fixed prefix abb followed by any number of a's and b's
questions.shortExplanation: Any prefix followed by the fixed suffix abb.
questions.explanation: `(a|b)*` matches any string, and the trailing `abb` fixes the ending, so the language is all strings ending in abb.

questions.text: Which identity is INVALID for regular expressions?
options: r** = r*, since the outer star is idempotent over closure
(r*)* = r*, because repeating closure adds no new strings
(rs)*r = r(sr)*, by shifting the leading r across the repetition
questions.shortExplanation: (r|s)* ≠ r*|s* in general.
questions.explanation: `(r|s)*` allows interleaving of r and s, while `r*|s*` allows only all-r or all-s strings; e.g. 'rs' is in the former but not the latter.

questions.text: The ε-closure of a state q in an NFA is:
options: The set of states reachable from q using only ε-transitions (including q)
The single state q with no other states ever included in the set
The complete set of all accepting states found anywhere in the NFA
The set of states reachable from q after consuming exactly one non-ε input symbol
questions.shortExplanation: ε-closure = states reachable via ε-moves, including q itself.
questions.explanation: ε-closure(q) contains q and every state reachable by following zero or more ε-transitions; it is central to subset construction.

questions.text: Which language over {a,b} is NOT regular?
options: Strings whose total length is exactly divisible by three
Strings containing the substring 'ab' at least once somewhere inside them
Strings of the form aⁿbⁿ for n ≥ 0
Strings that contain an even number of a's anywhere in the string
questions.shortExplanation: aⁿbⁿ needs counting → not regular.
questions.explanation: Matching equal numbers of a's and b's requires unbounded counting, which a finite automaton cannot do; the others are all regular.

questions.text: Two DFA states p and q are distinguishable if:
options: They happen to have exactly the same number of outgoing labelled edges
They are both accepting states reachable from the start
They were assigned the same textual label during construction
Some string leads one to an accepting state and the other to a non-accepting state
questions.shortExplanation: Distinguishable = some string separates accept/reject.
questions.explanation: States are distinguishable when there exists an input string after which one ends in an accepting state and the other does not; indistinguishable states merge in minimization.

questions.text: The longest-match rule combined with rule priority resolves the lexing of `<=` in a language with tokens `<`, `=`, and `<=` by:
options: Reporting a lexical error since two operators cannot be adjacent
Emitting `=` followed by `<` after reversing the character order
Emitting a single `<=` token because it is the longest match
Emitting `<` first and then `=` because those single-character tokens are listed earliest in the specification
questions.shortExplanation: Longest match prefers the two-character token.
questions.explanation: Maximal munch selects the longest lexeme that matches some pattern, so `<=` is recognized as one token rather than two separate ones.

questions.text: A scanner needs lookahead (and possibly retraction) primarily because:
options: It must read ahead to know whether a longer lexeme matches, then back up if not
The parser is structurally incapable of accepting any tokens at all
Every token in the language is guaranteed to be exactly one character long
Comments in the source are never stripped out by the scanner
questions.shortExplanation: Lookahead decides longest match; retract if overshoot.
questions.explanation: To honor longest-match the scanner reads beyond the current lexeme; if the extra characters do not extend a valid token it retracts to the last accepting position.

questions.text: If a regular language L is recognized by a DFA with k states, the Myhill–Nerode view says the minimal DFA has a number of states equal to the number of:
options: Symbols that appear in the input alphabet of the machine
Equivalence classes of the indistinguishability relation on states
Distinct labelled transitions present in the original unminimized DFA
Accepting states retained after the construction finishes
questions.shortExplanation: Minimal DFA states = indistinguishability equivalence classes.
questions.explanation: Minimization merges indistinguishable states; the minimal DFA has exactly one state per equivalence class of the indistinguishability relation.

questions.text: Which statement comparing NFA and DFA is FALSE?
options: An NFA may be exponentially smaller than the equivalent DFA
Both an NFA and a DFA recognize exactly the class of regular languages
A DFA can have an ε-transition to reduce its state count
Every NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA by subset construction
questions.shortExplanation: DFAs cannot have ε-transitions.
questions.explanation: By definition a DFA has no ε-transitions and exactly one move per symbol; the other statements are all true.

questions.text: The token, in the pair returned to the parser, is best thought of as a terminal symbol whose attribute most commonly carries:
options: The grammar production that the parser will eventually apply
The very next token that the scanner is about to read
The complete text of the source line on which the token was found
A pointer/index to additional information such as the symbol-table entry or numeric value
questions.shortExplanation: Attribute = handle to extra info (symbol-table ptr / value).
questions.explanation: The token name acts as the parser's terminal; the attribute value supplies extra data, e.g. a symbol-table pointer for ids or the numeric value for constants.

questions.text: Recognizing the keyword `if` instead of an identifier is usually handled MOST efficiently by:
options: Forbidding any identifier in the program from starting with the letter 'i'
Scanning identifiers normally, then checking a reserved-word table
Allowing the parser to reclassify the token much later during parsing
Building a completely separate dedicated DFA for each individual keyword in the language
questions.shortExplanation: Scan as id, then look up in a keyword table.
questions.explanation: It is simplest to match the identifier pattern and then consult a fixed table of reserved words, reclassifying the token if it matches a keyword.

questions.text: A DFA that recognizes 'strings over {0,1} with the number of 1s ≡ 0 (mod 3)' needs at least:
options: Only 1 state that loops on every input symbol
Exactly 2 states, one accepting and one rejecting
3 states
Infinitely many states to track the unbounded count of 1s
questions.shortExplanation: Three residues mod 3 → three states.
questions.explanation: The DFA must track the count of 1s modulo 3, requiring three distinct states (residues 0,1,2), with state 0 accepting.

questions.text: Thompson's construction is notable because the NFA it builds for a regular expression with size m has:
options: A number of states that grows exponentially in the size m of the expression
O(m) states and transitions, built compositionally
Exactly two states no matter how large m becomes
No ε-transitions of any kind connecting its fragments
questions.shortExplanation: Thompson NFA is linear in regex size, with ε-moves.
questions.explanation: Thompson's construction composes small NFA fragments per operator, producing O(m) states/transitions and using ε-transitions to glue them.

questions.text: Which pair of strings shows that `a*b*` is NOT the language 'equal numbers of a's then b's'?
options: the empty string '' is rejected by a*b* because it has no symbols
'aabbb' is accepted by a*b* but has unequal counts
'ab' is accepted by both languages and so proves they are identical
'ba' is accepted by a*b* even though the b precedes the a
questions.shortExplanation: a*b* allows unequal counts like aabbb.
questions.explanation: `a*b*` accepts any a's followed by any b's regardless of counts; 'aabbb' (2 a's, 3 b's) is accepted, so it is not the equal-count language.

questions.text: In a transition table for a DFA, an entry for (state, symbol) being empty/undefined means the scanner should:
options: Dynamically create a brand new state at run time to continue
Stay and loop in the very same state until a defined transition appears
Immediately accept the input as a valid complete lexeme
Treat it as a transition to a dead state and reject (or retract to last accept)
questions.shortExplanation: Missing transition = dead state / reject.
questions.explanation: An undefined transition conceptually goes to a non-accepting dead state; the scanner rejects or backs up to the most recent accepting configuration.

questions.text: Which is a correct ordering of the standard scanner-generation pipeline?
options: NFA → regular expression → DFA → minimal DFA, recovering the expression first
DFA → NFA → regular expression → minimal DFA, working backwards from the machine
Regular expression → DFA → NFA → minimal DFA, building the DFA before the NFA
Regular expression → NFA → DFA → minimal DFA
questions.shortExplanation: RE → NFA (Thompson) → DFA (subset) → minimize.
questions.explanation: The classic pipeline converts the RE to an NFA, then to a DFA by subset construction, then minimizes the DFA.

questions.text: The regular expression `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` describes:
options: An integer constant consisting solely of one or more decimal digits
A string literal enclosed between matching quotation marks
A floating-point literal with a decimal point and fractional digits
A typical identifier
questions.shortExplanation: Letter/underscore then letters/digits/underscores = identifier.
questions.explanation: It requires a leading letter or underscore followed by zero or more letters, digits, or underscores — the usual identifier pattern.

questions.text: Why are regular expressions chosen for tokens but context-free grammars for syntax?
options: Token structure is non-recursive and finite-state, while nested syntax needs the extra power of CFGs
Context-free grammars are fundamentally unable to describe identifiers
Finite automata always run more slowly at runtime than table-driven parsers
Regular expressions simply require fewer keystrokes for a programmer to type out
questions.shortExplanation: Tokens are regular; nesting needs CFG power.
questions.explanation: Lexical structure is non-recursive and recognizable by finite automata, whereas nested/balanced constructs require the greater power of context-free grammars.

questions.text: Buffer pairs with sentinels reduce per-character overhead mainly by:
options: Letting one comparison detect both buffer end and end-of-file via a sentinel
Keeping the entire contents of the source file permanently in CPU registers
Compressing the source code so that fewer characters must be examined
Eliminating the DFA so the scanner needs no transition logic at all
questions.shortExplanation: Sentinel merges end-of-buffer and EOF tests into one.
questions.explanation: Placing a sentinel (e.g., EOF) at each buffer half lets the inner loop test a single condition instead of two, cutting overhead.

questions.text: Which language is regular?
options: { w ∈ {a,b}* : w contains 'aba' as a substring }
{ wwᴿ : w ∈ {a,b}* }, the set of even-length palindromes over the alphabet
{ w : w has an equal number of a's and of b's anywhere in it }
{ aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0 }, with three equal-length blocks in order
questions.shortExplanation: Substring search is regular; the others need counting/matching.
questions.explanation: Detecting a fixed substring is recognizable by a finite automaton, while palindromes, aⁿbⁿcⁿ, and equal-count languages are not regular.

questions.text: A 'dead state' added to make a DFA total (fully specified) is:
options: An accepting state that happens to have no incoming edges directed into it
A state that can only ever be reached by following an ε-transition
A non-accepting trap state from which acceptance is unreachable
The designated start state of the automaton before any input
questions.shortExplanation: Dead state = non-accepting trap.
questions.explanation: Completing a partial DFA routes all missing transitions to a non-accepting trap (dead) state that loops on every symbol.

questions.text: Which best distinguishes a pattern from a lexeme?
options: A lexeme is the token's category while a pattern is merely its attribute value
A pattern is the concrete matched text, whereas a lexeme is the abstract rule describing it
The two terms are exact synonyms and may be used interchangeably
A pattern is the rule describing possible lexemes; a lexeme is a specific matched string
questions.shortExplanation: Pattern = rule; lexeme = actual matched string.
questions.explanation: The pattern (often a regular expression) specifies the form of acceptable strings; a lexeme is one concrete string instance that matches it.

questions.text: The number of accepting states in a minimal DFA for a nonempty regular language is:
options: Always zero, since minimization removes every accepting state
At least one, but possibly more
Always precisely equal to the number of symbols in the alphabet
Always exactly one, because minimization forces every accepting state to merge into a single one
questions.shortExplanation: Minimal DFA can have several accepting states.
questions.explanation: Minimization does not force a single accepting state; a minimal DFA may retain multiple accepting states if they are mutually distinguishable.

questions.text: Handling nested comments such as `/* ... /* ... */ ... */` correctly is impossible with a pure finite automaton because it requires:
options: Extending the input alphabet with extra comment delimiter symbols
Simply adding a few more accepting states to the existing transition diagram
Replacing the transition table with a noticeably faster lookup structure
Counting nesting depth, which exceeds finite-state memory
questions.shortExplanation: Nesting depth needs unbounded counting.
questions.explanation: Arbitrary nesting requires tracking depth without bound, which a finite-state machine cannot do; it needs at least a counter/stack.

questions.text: Given tokens for `relop` like `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `=`, `<>`, the transition diagram uses a final state with a '*' to indicate that the scanner has:
options: Read one extra character and must retract the input pointer by one
Consumed the entire remaining contents of the input file
Returned all the way back to the diagram's start state
Detected an illegal character and must abort with a reported lexical error
questions.shortExplanation: Starred final state means retract one character.
questions.explanation: A starred accepting state in a transition diagram marks that lookahead consumed an extra character which must be pushed back (retracted) after recognizing the token.

questions.text: Closure properties: the regular languages are closed under complement, which can be shown for a DFA by:
options: Deleting the start state so no input is ever accepted
Swapping accepting and non-accepting states of a complete DFA
Inserting ε-transitions between every pair of states in the machine
Reversing the direction of every transition and exchanging start and final roles
questions.shortExplanation: Complement = flip accepting/non-accepting on a total DFA.
questions.explanation: For a complete (total) DFA, exchanging accepting and non-accepting states yields a DFA for the complement language, proving closure under complement.

questions.text: Which scenario genuinely requires more than one character of lookahead in classical lexing?
options: Reading a one-digit decimal number that occupies just one character
Disambiguating constructs like Fortran 'DO 5 I = 1,5' vs 'DO5I = 1.5' where a later character decides the token
Recognizing a single-character arithmetic operator that stands entirely on its own
Skipping over a single isolated blank space between two tokens
questions.shortExplanation: Fortran DO-loop needs lookahead past the current lexeme.
questions.explanation: The classic Fortran example shows that whether 'DO' begins a loop or an assignment depends on a later comma/period, requiring extended lookahead.

questions.text: If two regular expressions r and s satisfy L(r) = L(s), then their minimal DFAs are:
options: Always different in their total number of states despite recognizing the same language
Completely unrelated to one another in structure
Isomorphic (identical up to state renaming)
Guaranteed to still contain at least one ε-transition apiece
questions.shortExplanation: Minimal DFA is unique up to isomorphism.
questions.explanation: For a given regular language the minimal DFA is unique up to renaming of states, so equal languages give isomorphic minimal DFAs.

questions.text: The lexical analyzer typically does NOT:
options: Verify that parentheses are balanced
Strip white space and comments from the stream before tokens reach the parser
Enter newly seen identifiers into the symbol table as it scans them
Attach line-number information to each token for later error reporting
questions.shortExplanation: Balancing parentheses is the parser's job, not the scanner's.
questions.explanation: Balanced nesting is a context-free property checked by the parser; the scanner handles white space, symbol-table entry, and bookkeeping like line numbers.
